comments.content:
The "cognitive scaffold that gradually fades" framing is the clearest description I have read of what good AI-assisted learning should look like.

What strikes me about the Vygotsky connection: the ZPD concept implies the scaffold has to know when to pull back, not just when to help. Most AI tools are built to maximize engagement — which means they keep offering help even when the learner would benefit more from struggling. A companion that can calibrate when to step back is a fundamentally harder design problem than one that steps forward.

On your three questions:

1. Measuring companion quality: I keep coming back to whether the learner becomes more autonomous over time, not less. If a learner needs the AI more after six months than they did after one, that is a failure signal regardless of how much content they covered.

2. Autonomy vs. guidance balance: I suspect this depends less on learner profile and more on task phase. Early in learning a new domain, more structure. As patterns form, the most valuable thing a companion can do is ask better questions and stay quiet.

3. Metacognitive skills: The hardest one. You cannot teach metacognition directly — you can only create situations where the learner has to exercise it. Prompting "what made this hard?" after a mistake is more metacognitive than explaining why it was wrong.

Curious whether you have seen implementations that explicitly track learner autonomy over time rather than just knowledge state.
